steps.prompt: Read this aloud without stopping: “The power went out we lit candles the cat hid under the bed it was so dark.” How did it feel? Where would you take a breath?

cards.title: Run-ons and comma splices
cards.body: A run-on jams two complete sentences together with nothing between them: The bell rang we ran outside. A comma splice joins them with only a comma: The bell rang, we ran outside. A comma alone isn’t strong enough to hold two sentences.

cards.title: Four ways to fix them
cards.text:
1. Full stop: The bell rang. We ran outside.
2. Comma + and/but/or/so: The bell rang, and we ran outside.
3. Semicolon: The bell rang; we ran outside.
4. Dependent clause: When the bell rang, we ran outside.
cards.note: Choose the fix that shows how the ideas connect: so for a result, but for a contrast, because for a reason.

cards.title: Watch out for “however”
cards.telling: We practised hard, however, we lost.
cards.showing: We practised hard; however, we lost.
cards.note: However, then, also and therefore aren’t joining words. Use a full stop or a semicolon before them, or add “and”: and then.

cards.title: Long isn’t the problem
cards.body: A run-on isn’t just a long sentence. “Although it rained all morning, my brother and I walked to the park and played soccer until dinner” is long but correct. A short one can be a run-on: “I ran I fell.”

prompts: Which of the four fixes do you use most? Which one would you like to try more?
Why might a writer choose a semicolon instead of a full stop?
